opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one where my own thinking has shifted over time. If you'd asked me a few years ago, I probably would have said tactile sensing is going to be essential, because when you watch people manipulate objects, so much of it seems to rely on touch. Think about finding your keys in your pocket, or buttoning a shirt.

What we've found in practice is that vision gets you surprisingly far. A lot of the tasks we've worked on, like folding laundry, bussing tables, or packing items into boxes, can be done quite well with just cameras, including wrist cameras that give a close-up view of the gripper and the object. The wrist camera picks up a lot of what you might think you'd need touch for: you can see whether the gripper has made contact, whether the object is slipping, how a cloth is deforming. So vision often serves as a decent proxy for tactile information.

There's also a very practical side. Cameras are cheap, robust, and standardized, and there's a huge amount of visual data out there plus pretrained vision-language models we can build on. Tactile sensors are still more fragile, more expensive, less standardized, and there isn't a big pretraining corpus for touch. So adding tactile sensing today means real costs in hardware and data, and you have to ask whether it's actually the bottleneck for the tasks you care about.

That said, I don't think tactile is unimportant. There are definitely tasks where it matters a lot: when the relevant contact is occluded, like reaching into a bag or a cluttered bin, really fine-grained insertion, or delicate manipulation where force matters, like handling fragile objects. In those cases vision just doesn't give you the signal you need.

So the way I assess it is mostly empirical: look at where our policies are failing and ask whether the failure is due to missing sensory information or something else, like not enough data, the model's reasoning, or the controller. Right now, for most of what we see, the bottleneck isn't the lack of touch, it's more about data and generalization. But as the systems get more capable and we push into more dexterous, contact-rich tasks, I'd expect tactile sensing to become increasingly valuable, especially if the sensors get cheaper and more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says wrist cameras reveal contact, slipping, and object deformation, allowing vision to serve as a decent proxy for tactile information.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot. The short answer is that vision does an enormous amount of the heavy lifting, and tactile sensing is valuable but in a much narrower set of situations than people often assume.

The reason vision is so dominant is partly about the information it carries and partly about data. A camera gives you a really rich view of the scene, where objects are, what state they're in, what the robot's own arm is doing, and you get all of that from a sensor that's cheap, robust, and that basically every robot can carry. And crucially, there's a huge amount of visual data in the world. When we think about pretraining and leveraging internet-scale data, that's all images and video. There's essentially no internet of touch. So if you want to build generalist policies, vision is the modality that lets you pull in all of that prior knowledge.

And honestly, you can go surprisingly far with vision alone. People sometimes underestimate how much contact information is actually visible. If the robot is folding a shirt or wiping a table, you can see when the gripper has made contact, you can see the cloth deform, you can see if something slipped. A policy trained end to end on image observations picks up on those cues even if nobody explicitly told it to.

Where tactile sensing starts to matter is when the thing you care about is occluded or just isn't visible. Grasping something inside a bag, feeling whether a connector has seated, inserting a key, judging how hard you're squeezing a soft object so you don't crush it. In those cases the camera really can't tell you what's going on at the fingertips, and force or tactile feedback fills that gap. We've found that even very simple signals, like force-torque at the wrist or gripper effort, give you a lot of that benefit without needing fancy fingertip sensors.

The practical challenge with richer tactile sensors is that they tend to be fragile, they wear out, they're hard to calibrate consistently across robots, and the data you collect on one sensor often doesn't transfer to another. That hurts you a lot when your whole approach depends on aggregating large datasets across many robots over long periods of time.

So the way I'd frame it is, vision is the foundation, and we treat touch as a complementary signal we add when the task demands it, ideally in the simplest form that gets the job done. I do think as tactile hardware gets more robust and standardized, it'll become a bigger part of the picture, especially for dexterous in-hand manipulation. But right now, if I had to pick one, it's not close.

r001.rationale: The response says vision can reveal contact, deformation, and slipping, but it does not mention wrist-mounted RGB cameras or clearly connect that camera setup to providing much of the information from tactile sensors.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Vision gives you a lot of information before you make contact: where an object is, what shape it is, how you might approach it. But once you’re interacting with it, there are things that are really difficult to infer visually. Is the object slipping? How much force are you applying? Have you actually made contact?

You can get surprisingly far with vision, and that makes it a useful place to start. But for more dexterous manipulation, I think touch becomes really valuable. If you’re trying to pick up something delicate or adjust an object within your hand, you want feedback about what’s happening at that contact point. So the question is less which sensor is better and more what information the task requires, and how the robot can combine those signals.

r001.rationale: The response describes vision and touch as complementary and identifies distinct information each provides, but it does not suggest that wrist-mounted RGB cameras provide much of the same information as tactile sensors.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Vision gives you a lot of information before you make contact: where an object is, its shape, and how you might grasp it. But once you’re interacting with it, there are things that are hard to infer visually. Is it slipping? How much force are you applying? Have you actually made contact?

Tactile sensing can be really valuable for those questions, especially when your hand is occluding what you’re doing. You can imagine picking up a delicate object or manipulating something inside a bag, where a camera just doesn’t have the right view.

The interesting question is how to get robots to learn to use both. You want vision to guide the interaction, and then touch to help the robot adjust as it goes.

r001.rationale: The response describes vision and touch as complementary, and says visual inference is difficult for slipping, force, and contact. It does not suggest that wrist-mounted RGB cameras provide much of the same information as tactile sensors.
